short: The UK has no AI act. AI is governed through UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, whose new automated-decision rules (Articles 22A to 22C) apply from 5 February 2026, and through sector regulators; AI policy moved to the Cabinet Office in July 2026.
title: United Kingdom AI Laws
subtitle: No AI act: UK GDPR, the new automated-decision rules and sector regulators
body_html:
Status at a glance

No AI act; privacy and sector law bind. The UK has no comprehensive AI statute and has not announced one. AI is governed through data protection law, which the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amended with new rules on automated decision-making in force since 5 February 2026, and through the existing sector regulators. On 22 July 2026 the government announced that "responsibility for AI strategy, public sector AI adoption and the AI Security Institute will move to the Cabinet Office", with the functions of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology redistributed. In October 2026 the AI minister named the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as the vehicle for AI-driven cyber and loss-of-control risks; no AI bill has been introduced. Verified on 25 October 2026 against GOV.UK and legislation.gov.uk.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumberPassedIn force
Data (Use and Access) Act 20252025 c. 18Royal Assent 19 June 2025In stages; s. 80, automated decision-making, from 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82)
UK GDPRRegulation (EU) 2016/679 as retainedIn force
Data Protection Act 20182018 c. 12In force

Who regulates and enforces

  • Information Commissioner's Office (ICO): data protection, including the automated-decision rules.
  • Cabinet Office: AI strategy, public-sector AI adoption and the AI Security Institute, from the July 2026 machinery-of-government change.
  • AI Security Institute: renamed from the AI Safety Institute on 14 February 2025; security research, not a regulator.
  • Sector regulators such as the FCA, CMA, MHRA and Ofcom apply their own rules to AI within their remits.

Scope and reach

UK GDPR applies to controllers and processors established in the UK, wherever the processing happens, and to those outside the UK whose processing relates to offering goods or services to people in the UK or monitoring their behaviour in the UK (Art. 3(1) and (2)). The trigger is where the people are.

Core obligations

  • UK GDPR Articles 22A (automated processing and significant decisions), 22B (restrictions on automated decision-making) and 22C (safeguards), inserted by section 80 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
  • The rest of UK GDPR and the DPA 2018, and each sector regulator's rulebook.

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Higher-tier data protection infringementsGBP 17,500,000 or 4% of the undertaking's total annual worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year, whichever is higherDPA 2018 s. 157(5)ICO
Standard-tier infringementsGBP 8,700,000 or 2% of total annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higherDPA 2018 s. 157(6)ICO

What is coming next

  • The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, named by the AI minister on 12 October 2026 for AI-driven cyber and loss-of-control risks.
  • The remaining commencement regulations of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

The rulebook that applies in practice

With no AI act, the duties that reach an AI deployer in the UK come from four places, each with its own regulator. First, the UK GDPR as rewritten by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: section 80 replaced Article 22 with new Articles 22A to 22D on 5 February 2026, under the Commencement No. 6 Regulations made on 29 January 2026, loosening the ban on solely automated decisions while keeping safeguards (information, a right to make representations, human intervention) for decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. The ICO opened a consultation on draft guidance interpreting those articles on 31 March 2026, closing 29 May, and published a report on automated decision-making in recruitment the same day; in January 2026 the government said a statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making would follow, which law-firm commentary expects in 2027. The ICO's 2026 priorities, set out in its June 2025 AI and biometrics strategy, are foundation-model developers (an engagement programme with eleven of them), automated decision-making in recruitment and central government, and police use of facial recognition, where it has audited five forces and plans a final audit of the Metropolitan Police. PECR fines were raised to the GDPR level of £17.5 million or 4% of global turnover.

Second, Ofcom under the Online Safety Act 2023, which the government has said it will amend so that AI chatbots are inside the regime and so that creating a non-consensual intimate deepfake, criminalised by the Data (Use and Access) Act, becomes a priority offence alongside sharing one. Third, the sector regulators, each now publishing AI expectations: the FCA through the Consumer Duty and a planned joint code with the ICO, the MHRA for AI medical devices, Ofgem for the energy sector, the CMA's data and technology unit, and the SRA for legal services. Fourth, the Equality Act 2010, enforced by the EHRC and the tribunals, which is where most discrimination-by-algorithm claims will actually be brought.

The legislative vehicles named for 2026 and 2027 are not AI-safety bills. The King's Speech announced a Regulating for Growth Bill carrying cross-economy regulatory sandboxes, an AI Growth Lab and a growth duty on regulators; the ICO has separately published research on a statutory data protection sandbox that would grant time-limited derogations. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which the AI minister named in October 2026 as the home for AI-driven cyber risk, widens the scope and duties of the 2018 NIS Regulations. A private member's AI (Regulation) Bill has been reintroduced in the Lords in each session and has not progressed. The AI Security Institute, renamed from Safety in 2025, tests frontier models and signs international agreements but enforces nothing.

The commencement regulations and the ICO consultation dates are as Osborne Clarke and Covington report them, consistent with the GOV.UK reading of 25 October; the King's Speech bill, the Online Safety Act amendments and the sector-regulator list are reported from law-firm notes, not read on GOV.UK, and are reported rather than verified. Not checked one by one: each sector regulator's AI remit.
